## A report is more than a result {#sec-intro}

This is a working tour of Cairn reports: **pinned evidence**, *executable analysis*,
structured tables, figures, mathematics, and playable media. Select this paragraph
and use the copy button to copy its text together with its source marker.

The report is rendered from its intermediate document, with one page scrollbar.
Every output below belongs to this published version.[^evidence]

> Good reports let a reader move from a claim to the evidence that supports it.

{{< include includes/method.qmd >}}

## Standard code blocks {#sec-standard-code}

Ordinary fenced code is shown with syntax highlighting and is **never executed**.
These examples describe a workflow; only the report's `{python}` cells execute.

```python
from cairn import Client

# A display-only example, not an executed report cell.
def summarize(values: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(values) / len(values)

print("This code fence is not executed")
```

```javascript
const state = { selected: true, threshold: 0.05 };
const visible = samples.filter(sample => sample.loss < state.threshold);
console.log(`Showing ${visible.length} samples`);
```

```yaml
experiment:
  name: adaptive-wave
  seed: 42
  features:
    - pinned-inputs
    - interactive-plots
```

```text
Plain text remains plain: <script>this is displayed, not executed</script>
```

## Pinned experiment inputs {#sec-inputs}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-result
#| tbl-cap: Final values from the pinned baseline.
import base64
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display, HTML, Markdown
result = inputs["baseline"].read()
display({"application/json": result}, raw=True)
```

The exact input versions are available in the **Lineage** tab. The configuration,
environment, and report sources remain inspectable in the metadata and files views.

## Tables and structured output {#sec-tables}

| Feature | Source | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static table | Markdown | Native table layout |
| Rich table | Python HTML | Sanitized, in the document flow |
| JSON | Python MIME output | Inspectable structured result |

```{python}
#| label: tbl-comparison
#| tbl-cap: A table generated from the captured CSV resource.
rows = list(csv.DictReader(Path("data.csv").open()))
headers = list(rows[0])
body = "<table><thead><tr>" + "".join(f"<th>{key}</th>" for key in headers) + "</tr></thead><tbody>"
for row in rows:
    body += "<tr>" + "".join(f"<td>{row[key]}</td>" for key in headers) + "</tr>"
display(HTML(body + "</tbody></table>"))
```

As @tbl-comparison shows, the adaptive method has the lowest illustrative loss.
These values are synthetic demonstration data, not experimental findings.

## Images and convergence {#sec-figures}

![The wave field at the beginning of the sequence.](assets/field-start.png){#fig-start}

```{python}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: Scalar loss from the pinned experiment.
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
records = inputs["baseline"].records()
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.3))
figure.patch.set_facecolor("#fffef9")
axis.set_facecolor("#fffef9")
axis.plot([row["data"]["step"] for row in records], [row["data"]["loss"] for row in records], color="#176b5b", linewidth=2)
axis.set(xlabel="Step", ylabel="Loss", title="A steady convergence")
axis.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
figure.tight_layout()
display(figure)
plt.close(figure)
```

Compare @fig-start with the animation below. @fig-convergence demonstrates an
executed figure output, while the first image is a captured source resource.

## Interactive exploration {#sec-plotly}

Hover over a point for exact values, drag to zoom, and double-click to reset.
Click legend entries to compare methods, or export the figure as SVG using the toolbar.
The reader applies Cairn colors, typography, and grid styling by default.

```{python}
#| label: fig-interactive
#| fig-cap: Interactive convergence comparison with synthetic baseline and adaptive traces.
#| echo: false
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import math
steps = list(range(60))
interactive = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=steps, y=[math.exp(-s / 18) + .02 for s in steps], name="Baseline", mode="lines"),
    go.Scatter(x=steps, y=[math.exp(-s / 12) + .015 for s in steps], name="Adaptive", mode="lines"),
])
interactive.update_layout(title="Convergence comparison", xaxis_title="Training step", yaxis_title="Loss", legend={"orientation": "h", "y": -.25})
display({"application/vnd.plotly.v1+json": json.loads(interactive.to_json())}, raw=True)
```

## A small 3D surface {#sec-plotly-3d}

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and hover to inspect the height of this synthetic field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-surface
#| fig-cap: A small interactive Plotly 3D wave surface.
#| echo: false
coords = [i / 10 - 2 for i in range(41)]
surface = go.Figure(go.Surface(
    x=coords, y=coords,
    z=[[math.sin(x * 2) * math.cos(y * 2) * math.exp(-(x*x+y*y)/5) for x in coords] for y in coords],
    colorscale=[[0, "#176b5b"], [.5, "#dcebe5"], [1, "#b56231"]],
    showscale=False,
))
surface.update_layout(title="A wave field in three dimensions", height=380,
    scene={"xaxis_title": "x", "yaxis_title": "y", "zaxis_title": "Amplitude",
           "camera": {"eye": {"x": 1.5, "y": 1.5, "z": 1}}})
display({"application/vnd.plotly.v1+json": json.loads(surface.to_json())}, raw=True)
```

## Custom HTML and WebGPU {#sec-custom-html}

Custom HTML can implement an entirely different viewer. This example runs its own
JavaScript and WebGPU shader in an isolated frame, and automatically fits into the
report. Change the phase slider, then expand the details. If WebGPU is unavailable,
the same field renders through Canvas instead.

```{python}
#| label: fig-custom-html
#| fig-cap: A custom HTML viewer with optional WebGPU rendering.
#| echo: false
display(HTML(Path("assets/custom-viewer.html").read_text()))
```

## Video playback {#sec-video}

The synthetic wave field evolves over four seconds. Use the Prism2 playback
controls to play, pause, seek, mute, adjust volume, or enlarge and inspect frames.
In the lightbox, use the scissors tool to drag a time range on the timeline;
optionally use the region tool to draw a rectangle on the video. The copy icon
copies both selections in one source reference.

```{python}
#| label: fig-video
#| fig-cap: A synthetic wave field, 60 frames at 15 frames per second.
#| echo: false
display({"video/mp4": base64.b64encode(Path("assets/wave-evolution.mp4").read_bytes()).decode()}, raw=True)
```

## Audio playback {#sec-audio}

This two-second chirp illustrates native audio playback. It starts only when you
press play; adjust the volume using the player.

```{python}
#| echo: false
display({"audio/wav": base64.b64encode(Path("assets/signal.wav").read_bytes()).decode()}, raw=True)
```

## Reading checklist {#sec-checklist}

1. Inspect the pinned values in @tbl-result.
2. Compare the image and chart in @sec-figures.
3. Play the video and audio without leaving the report.
4. Copy text from @sec-method and confirm its included-file source marker.
5. Open **Lineage** to inspect input versions and downstream consumers.
6. Use **Files** to download the captured source, notebook, and media.

[^evidence]: Reports pin inputs before execution and publish their captured files as immutable evidence.
